title: The Imbued
summary: Ordinary people woken to the monsters around them.

claims.text: The imbued are hunters: people shown the real world, monsters and all, and given strange powers, it seems to oppose them.
Some call themselves the chosen, in relation to the Heralds.
They know very little about themselves, why they were woken or what they face, so they argue and guess; the shared terms come from those talks.
The common words were coined on the hidden hunter-net mailing list; isolated hunters do not know them and likely have their own.

title: The Messengers and the Heralds
summary: Whatever imbues the hunters.

claims.text: Messengers is a name for the forces thought to cause the imbuing; hunters of different cultures see them differently, but most think them good, or at least not evil.
Heralds is another name for the mysterious beings, likely many, thought to have empowered hunters; they are usually taken as agents of a higher power, often God.
To be touched is to be affected by the Messengers, whether hunter or bystander.

title: Bystanders and Other Witnesses
summary: The people at an imbuing who do not become hunters.

claims.text: A bystander sees the supernatural at an imbuing but lacks the will to act; they remember the monsters afterward but have no edges.
A pylon is a person at the scene who does not notice or respond to the monster; the term is unkind.
A gawker sees edges or monstrous powers at work but cannot understand them. The defenseless, or the blind, are people with no idea of the truth.

title: Creeds
summary: The approaches to the hunt that hunters see among themselves.

claims.text: Early hunter groups think the imbued share certain ways of hunting that could be set down as separate creeds.
Avengers above all want the supernatural wiped out; Defenders protect chosen people, places or things as much as they kill monsters.
Innocents come to the hunt with open, unjaded minds; Judges weigh how best to do the most good, by their own lights.
Martyrs will give themselves up for the cause; Redeemers look for worth among monsters instead of destroying them outright.
Visionaries take a thoughtful view of the hunt and assume little about the Heralds, monsters or what the chosen are for.

title: Edges
summary: The powers of the imbued.

claims.text: An edge is any of the strange powers of the imbued, also called the stuff, or juice.
Second sight, or the sight, is seeing monsters through force of will, even those that hide or disguise themselves.

title: The Word
summary: The hunters' code of signs.

claims.text: The imbued gain a language of symbols they read and write as if they always knew it; many call it the Word.
Each sign carries a short message, such as a safe house, a vampire's turf, or a neighbourhood under a hunter's guard; one to three signs make a message.
The signs appear mostly as graffiti, as directions and warnings, and new hunters use them to find others.
No one has catalogued them, and so far neither monsters nor their human pawns seem to notice them; if the code were broken, hunters would be badly exposed.

title: What Hunters Call Monsters
summary: The hunters' words for their enemy.

claims.text: Monster covers every inhuman creature that preys on people: rots, invisibles, bloodsuckers, skinchangers, ghosts, walking dead, witches and more; together they are the enemy.
The Most Dangerous Game is the hunt itself, and also the enemy, prey able to fight back.
A puppet, or traitor, is a human pawn of the supernatural, knowing or not.
The soulless are people who admire the supernatural or help it by doubtful behaviour; the word depends wholly on the speaker's morals, and some hunters call other hunters soulless.

title: Hunter Slang
summary: Words for kinds of hunter and ways of hunting.

claims.text: The hunt, or the mission, is the hunter's life: pursuing, tracking, studying and finally facing the supernatural.
Bait use themselves as lures; lurkers research online but stay out of the hunt, and are sneered at as wannabes.
Gone fishing is said of hunters who flee the city for quiet countryside. A wacko takes the mission to extremes of sacrifice or loss.
A yokel trusts folk tales about monsters, often without testing them. The burden is humanity, above all those who would keep society's evils rather than risk change.

title: Conviction and the Virtues
summary: A hunter's staying power, and the three aims of the hunt.

claims.text: Conviction measures a hunter's endurance for the hunt and is the store of energy spent on edges; the starting amount depends on the creed.
Spending a point of Conviction lets the second sight find monsters hidden nearby, such as one using powers to disguise itself; anyone can see monsters that are not hiding.
Second sight also marks every supernatural being as not human or not living; spirits in the material world look solid to the hunter.
The three Virtues are Mercy, Vision and Zeal. Mercy goes with Innocents, Martyrs and Redeemers; Vision with Visionaries; Zeal with Defenders, Judges and Avengers.
A creed is not a club or class a hunter joins but how that hunter sees and carries out the mission; the main Virtue shows what the hunter holds as the war's goal.

title: Avengers
summary: The Zeal creed that wants every monster punished.

claims.text: Followers of Vengeance are mostly called Avengers, though punishers, executioners and slayers are also heard; in the American bible belt some call them soldiers of God.
They are driven to settle the score: evil has to pay and no deal with it is acceptable.
Their known weakness is extremism, which may have drawn them to the hunt and may also end their part in it.

title: Defenders
summary: The Zeal creed that guards home and loved ones.

claims.text: Defenders see themselves as unwilling fighters who still hold firm; they leave the chase to others and keep hearth and home safe above all.
They warn that a Defender who loses loved ones is likely to give in to anger and may become a danger in turn.
Their usual failing is retreat into isolation: fortifying a home is routine among hunters, but refusing to leave one out of fear is a sign to get help.

title: Innocents
summary: The Mercy creed that comes to the hunt without assumptions.

claims.text: Many Innocents are young, but age sets no limit; they take up the hunt with no fixed ideas about it.
More than other hunters they live in the present, without old grudges or plans for later, and like the other Mercy creeds they see kin in the monsters.
Their weakness is guilt: when they must hurt someone, or help a friend do it, the guilt can stop them cold.

title: Judges
summary: The Zeal creed that weighs each case.

claims.text: Judges stand between Avengers, who punish the guilty, and Defenders, who pick out what to save; they come forward when the thing cannot be allowed to go on but the greatest good is unclear.
Their weakness is indecision, which lets others push them aside; the opposite failing is megalomania, the belief that only the Judge knows what is right.

title: Martyrs
summary: The Mercy creed that gives itself up for others.

claims.text: Martyrs must destroy monsters yet know their prey has or once had human feelings; they lack the plain us and them view of Avengers.
For all that understanding they hunt with a fury close to self-destruction.
Their weakness is masochism: some keep on because they enjoy suffering, and are told their task is to hand out punishment, not to take it.

title: Redeemers
summary: The Mercy creed that tries to save what it hunts.

claims.text: Redeemers reach first for peace; they are prized for healing the injured but often clash with hunters whose aims differ.
Some try to understand their prey, hoping to calm haunting spirits or lift the curse or sickness behind a monster.
Their weaknesses are a messianic streak that can lead them away from the hunt toward a purer calling, and greed, beginning with paid miracles for the rich.

title: Visionaries
summary: The Vision creed that seeks to understand.

claims.text: Visionaries take the arrival of the uncanny in their lives as proof that the world is bigger and stranger than they thought.
They refuse to leap to conclusions or grab at half-made answers.
Other hunters call them Tunnel-Visionaries for fixing on small details and pet theories; addiction is another risk for those who chase understanding.

title: Edges of Innocence
summary: Mercy edges for hiding, seeing and holding monsters off.

claims.text: Hide: Wits + Mercy, difficulty 6; each monster present rolls Perception + Alertness, difficulty 6, to notice the hunter. A raging monster that passes over an obvious Innocent suggests Hide is at work.
Illuminate: Perception + Mercy. Monsters seem able to sense its use and can tell which person is behind it.
A radiating hunter (Stamina + Mercy, difficulty 6) raises the difficulty of any supernatural attack on the target by one per success.
Another edge costs one Conviction (Manipulation + Mercy, difficulty 5): each success makes an attacker spend a Willpower point to act against the hunter.
Blaze costs two Conviction (Strength + Mercy, difficulty 8) and turns a light source into lethal damage that depends on the light; it does not work with moonlight.

title: Edges of Martyrdom
summary: Mercy edges paid for with the hunter's own body.

claims.text: Demand lets the hunter perform a feat of great strength by marking a level of bashing damage on the hunter's own Health.
Witness builds on second sight: the hunter knows the nature of creatures present and glimpses their ties to humankind.
One edge harms a target within the hunter's Mercy in yards (Manipulation + Mercy, difficulty 7).
Donate costs two Conviction (Mercy + the Attribute lent, difficulty 7): the hunter gives up points of that Attribute to another person for a time.
One edge forces a human limit on a supernatural being, such as making a dead thing need to breathe or a ghost take solid form.

title: Edges of Redemption
summary: Mercy edges that shield, heal and calm.

claims.text: One edge shields another person from harm (Wits + Mercy, difficulty 6, usually resisted by the attack roll); the hunter must see the danger, and it cannot stop an avalanche or a lightning bolt.
Another makes a creature face people in human terms, bringing sorrow and loss; each success adds one to the difficulty of its next action (Manipulation + Mercy, difficulty 6).
Respire heals one health level per success (Stamina + Mercy, difficulty 6), and turned on a supernatural foe it draws energy out instead; even intangible foes are at risk.
Becalm costs one Conviction (Manipulation + Mercy, difficulty 7) and lasts minutes equal to successes; it stops only explosive or violent acts and binds the hunter and allies too.
One edge costs two Conviction (Charisma + Mercy, difficulty 8) and seals the material world off from every other realm.

title: Edges of Vision
summary: Edges of insight, foresight and the past.

claims.text: Foresee: Intelligence + Vision, difficulty 7; each success grants one extra roll for a named action, keeping the best result.
Pinpoint: Perception + Vision, difficulty 6; a success reveals one weakness of the creature watched. It does nothing to mortals.
Delve: Perception + Vision, difficulty 6; each success gives five minutes of viewing a place's past. Hearing as well costs two Conviction or two more difficulty.
One edge makes lethal damage count as bashing; it eases wounds but heals nothing.
Augur costs three Conviction; the Storyteller secretly rolls Intelligence + Vision, difficulty 8, and gives visions of likely futures at that spot.

title: Edges of Defense
summary: Zeal edges that guard, heal and draw foes away.

claims.text: Ward: Stamina + Zeal, difficulty 6; a monster must beat those successes on a Stamina roll to come near, and the aura crackles on contact.
Rejuvenate heals bashing levels at one per ten minutes and lethal ones by a chart, and the hunter can share the healing.
Brand needs a touch, perhaps a Dexterity + Brawl roll; ordinary people see the brand as an unsettling tattoo, and it does not work on objects or normal people.
Champion costs one Conviction (Appearance + Zeal) and needs the monster to keep the hunter in sight; it draws creatures off so others slip by or walk into an ambush, once per creature.
Burn costs two Conviction (Stamina + Zeal, difficulty 6) and lasts a turn per success; the hunter glows red and yellow and touching the hunter hurts.

title: Edges of Judgment
summary: Zeal edges that see, hold and expose.

claims.text: Discern is used to identify a supernatural creature or to see clearly in the dark.
Burden: the hunter glares (Stamina + Zeal) and holds the creature in place while it stays in view; travel to other realms or great speed may break free.
A spoken curse (Wits + Zeal against the foe's Stamina + 2) blocks the creature's supernatural powers and functions.
Pierce costs one Conviction for a scene and senses lies; it can also give silent visions of what an object, person or place has met.
Expose costs two Conviction (Zeal, difficulty 8), reaches farther with more successes and shows creatures for what they are; it is usable once a scene.

title: Edges of Vengeance
summary: Zeal edges for the fight.

claims.text: Cleave empowers a held melee weapon or makes one appear (Dexterity + Brawl or Melee to hit); only hunters and supernatural beings can see a manifested blade, and it never works on ranged weapons.
One edge, used by touching a target (Perception + Zeal, difficulty 6), leaves a trail the target cannot see without special senses.
A smolder cloud (Manipulation + Zeal, difficulty 7) fills about ten cubic feet and hides those inside from sight, smell, heat sense, most hearing and most supernatural awareness.
Another edge costs one Conviction and gives a pool equal to Zeal to share among Strength, Dexterity and the like.

One more costs one Conviction (Dexterity + Zeal, difficulty 6), adds successes past the first to a lethal Strength pool and goes off with light, noise and a stench that scramble electronics within 20 feet.

title: Reacting with Conviction
summary: Spending Conviction when danger shows itself.

claims.text: As an option, the Storyteller may let hunters spend Conviction when warning signs appear, rather than at the start of each scene.
The roll is Intelligence, Perception or Wits plus the primary Virtue, difficulty 6; the Storyteller picks the Attribute and may use Alertness, Awareness or Intuition in place of the Virtue.
The roll may be resisted by the creature's Stealth or its power, and the Storyteller may roll in secret.
Players should all know beforehand if this option is in use; hunters may still turn on the sight at will.

title: Conviction Against Lasting Control
summary: What Conviction does to powers that last for days.

claims.text: If Conviction is spent while a hunter is under long-lasting mind or body control, the Storyteller chooses: either the control breaks for good, or the hunter is free only for that scene.
The Storyteller may also let the spend reveal the hidden influence, so the hunter can seek help even if control returns later.

title: Primary Virtue Rolls Against Great Foes
summary: Testing whether a hunter's defenses hold against an ancient monster.

claims.text: Against a mighty enemy the Storyteller may call for a primary Virtue roll before the protections work: difficulty 6 for a strong foe, perhaps 8 for a titanic one.
On a success the hunter sees the creature's inhumanity and the usual protections apply; Willpower cannot buy an automatic success.
On a failure the hunter is no better off than an ordinary mortal against that foe, and the Storyteller decides whether to allow later tries.

title: Risking Conviction
summary: Betting Conviction on an edge roll.

claims.text: Edges that need Conviction to start are paid separately, and do not use up the one chance per scene to risk Conviction on a roll.
If the boosted roll succeeds, the hunter keeps the points risked and gains one more; in a contest the hunter must win.
If it fails, every point risked is lost; a hunter at zero Conviction is close to an ordinary person.
On a botch the hunter loses all current Conviction, and the hunt may feel empty for a while.

title: Reaching Ten Conviction
summary: Turning a full store of Conviction into a Virtue.

claims.text: Conviction runs from 1 to 10; at 10 the player may trade it for one extra Virtue point, gained at once.
No other Virtue may rise above the primary Virtue, though it may equal it.

title: Gaining Edges
summary: How hunters receive their powers.

claims.text: The Storyteller may let players choose edges at creation, or start them as plain people and grant a first edge after the prelude to match their reaction: violence might bring a weapon, scheming a stealthy power.
More edges come with more Virtue points; the Storyteller may let the player choose, or pick one and keep it hidden until a dramatic moment.

title: How Edges Look
summary: Who can see an edge at work.

claims.text: Hunters see the effects of their own and each other's edges, such as light from a fist, grey fog or wounds closing, and so do the monsters they fight.
With a Conviction point spent, a hunter sees supernatural beings as they really are, including those hiding in plain sight.
Ordinary people do not really grasp what they see, but hunters still cannot use edges openly without risk: people see the aftermath, and a beheading is still a beheading.
